title: Transportation & Driving
tagline: Trucking, delivery, transit, and aviation — the careers that keep people and goods moving.
summary: Transportation careers range from CDL trucking and last-mile delivery to transit operations, dispatch, and commercial aviation — licensed, safety-critical work with real demand and clear advancement from driver to owner-operator, dispatcher, or fleet leadership. This roadmap covers licenses, the lifestyle reality, and the branch points.

sources.label: O*NET — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers (53-3032.00)
BLS OOH — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers

detail.description: Moving people and goods spans trucking (long-haul, regional, local), delivery and last mile, transit and passenger service, warehousing crossover, and aviation — most entry roles license-based rather than degree-based.
detail.why: Transportation is one of the economy's largest employers with persistent driver demand — and one of the few careers where a license obtained in weeks becomes a lifetime skill.
learn: Read the BLS profile of heavy truck drivers
Compare local delivery vs regional vs long-haul lifestyles
Check which licenses your target roles require
Ride along or shadow one operation if possible

resources.title: BLS OOH — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers
O*NET — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers

detail.description: Driving licenses tier by vehicle: standard license, CDL Class B (heavier straight trucks, buses), CDL Class A (tractor-trailers) — each with knowledge tests, skills tests, medical certification, and endorsements.
detail.why: Understanding the license ladder tells you exactly what each career step requires — no guessing.
learn: Learn your state's CDL classes and what each allows
Understand the medical certificate (DOT physical) requirement
Note entry-level driver training (ELDT) requirements
Check endorsement options: HazMat, tanker, passenger, school bus

detail.description: The honest picture: long-haul means days or weeks away; regional means weekends home; local means daily home with city intensity. Sleep, meals, and health require deliberate management.
detail.why: Lifestyle fit predicts who thrives — choosing the segment that matches your life is the most important early decision.
learn: Compare time-away patterns across segments
Talk to 3 drivers: local, regional, OTR
Plan sleep and meal strategies for your target segment
Discuss the schedule honestly with your household

resources.title: BLS OOH — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers

detail.description: Transportation is safety-regulated end to end: vehicle inspections, hours-of-service rules, drug and alcohol testing programs, and CSA-style safety scores that follow drivers and carriers.
detail.why: Your safety record is your résumé in this industry — it determines employability, insurance, and advancement.
learn: Learn the vehicle inspection routine (pre/post-trip)
Understand hours-of-service basics before your first job
Know the drug-and-alcohol clearinghouse reality (US)
Keep your record clean from day one

detail.description: CDL paths: private trucking schools (weeks, paid upfront), company-sponsored training (contract commitments), and community-college programs — all ending in knowledge and skills tests.
detail.why: The CDL is the field's foundational credential; choosing the funding path wisely (beware of expensive contracts) is your first business decision.
learn: Compare school costs vs sponsored-training contracts
Get the DOT medical certificate early
Practice the pre-trip inspection until automatic
Check ELDT-compliant training providers

detail.description: First jobs: over-the-road team or solo with training carriers, regional hauls, or local routes if experience allows — the first year is about clean records and learning the logistics network.
detail.why: Year one builds the verified experience every better job requires; choosing decent first carriers matters more than chasing top cents-per-mile.
learn: Research carrier reputations with current drivers
Understand pay structures (CPM, percentage, hourly)
Track your record: inspections, on-time, fuel
Set a 12-month plan to your preferred segment

resources.title: BLS OOH — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers

tasks: Drive a tractor-trailer combination or a truck with a capacity of at least 26,000 GVW to transport and deliver goods or materials over land.

detail.description: Last-mile delivery (parcels, furniture, food supply) runs on routes and stops per day — physically intense, home nightly, with courier, gig, and company-employee models.
detail.why: Last-mile is the fastest-growing segment and the most local — ideal for drivers who want every night at home.
learn: Compare employee courier vs gig vs contracted routes
Learn safe delivery practices for residential stops
Understand package-handling standards for damage claims
Track a realistic stops-per-day pace

detail.description: Passenger roles include transit bus, school bus (passenger + school-bus endorsements), motorcoach, paratransit, and rideshare — people-first driving with fixed routes or scheduled service.
detail.why: Transit systems offer public-sector stability and pensions; school buses offer daytime hours that fit parenting schedules.
learn: Check your transit authority's hiring and training program
Get passenger and school-bus endorsements if targeting them
Learn customer-conflict de-escalation for the road
Note the different background checks for school transport

detail.description: CDL endorsements expand what you can haul: HazMat (with TSA background check), Tanker, Doubles/Triples, and Passenger — each is a test (and for HazMat, a security threat assessment).
detail.why: Endorsements are wage multipliers — tankers and HazMat pay premiums because they demand more responsibility.
learn: Prioritize Tanker + HazMat for pay premiums
Budget for the TSA HazMat background check
Study each endorsement's test content
Recertify/track expiration dates carefully

detail.description: Owner-operators own or lease their truck and run a business: authority, insurance, fuel and maintenance economics, load boards or contracts, and the discipline of saving for repairs.
detail.why: Ownership is the classic wealth path in trucking — but it runs on business skill as much as driving skill.
learn: Model cost-per-mile before leasing anything
Learn authority, insurance, and ELD requirements
Compare load boards vs contract freight
Keep a repair reserve fund from the first paycheck

detail.description: Dispatchers and fleet coordinators plan loads, routes, and driver schedules — solving problems by phone all day; fleet managers add maintenance, compliance, and budget responsibility.
detail.why: Dispatch is the natural desk-side promotion for drivers who know the road — and a standalone career for organizers.
learn: Learn load planning and HOS-aware scheduling
Practice driver communication under pressure
Understand ELD data and compliance reports
Shadow a dispatcher for a day

resources.title: BLS OOH — Material Recording Clerks and related

detail.description: Drivers who understand their equipment — daily inspections, fluids, tires, brakes, DEF systems — break down less and earn trust with mechanics and carriers; some transition into diesel-tech careers.
detail.why: Mechanical literacy saves money for owners and prevents the career-killing roadside failure.
learn: Master the pre-trip inspection system (not just the test)
Learn basic fluids, belts, and tire care
Understand ELD and diagnostics readouts
Consider diesel-technician training as a branch

resources.title: BLS OOH — Diesel Service Technicians and Mechanics

detail.description: Driving experience is valued in supply-chain roles — logistics coordinator, broker support, warehouse operations — see the Supply Chain & Logistics roadmap for the fuller network view.
detail.why: The road-to-desk crossover is well-trodden: drivers make excellent logistics professionals because they know reality.
learn: Learn shipper/carrier/receiver relationships from your seat
Take a logistics fundamentals course if interested
Note which desk roles value driving years
Keep a network of dispatchers and brokers

detail.description: Experienced drivers branch into safety and compliance roles: driver-manager, safety officer, DOT compliance specialist, and state/federal inspector paths.
detail.why: Safety careers value exactly what veteran drivers have: records, credibility, and regulatory fluency.
learn: Study FMCSA audit and compliance basics
Learn CSA score mechanics
Explore safety-officer postings at carriers
Note inspector roles in your state's enforcement agency

detail.description: Aviation careers: pilots (private → instrument → commercial → ATP through flight schools or airline academies), flight attendants, dispatchers, and airport operations — medical certificates and hour-building define the pilot path.
detail.why: Pilot demand is strong and the path is fully mapped — but expensive; financing strategy (academy vs part-61 vs military) is decision one.
learn: Take a discovery flight before committing
Compare Part 61 vs Part 141 training costs and timelines
Get the FAA medical certificate early (class 1/2)
Research airline cadet and tuition programs

resources.title: BLS OOH — Airline and Commercial Pilots

detail.description: Airline careers beyond the cockpit: flight attendants (safety-certified, schedule-built seniority), ramp and ground operations, gate agents, and airport management — seniority systems shape everything.
detail.why: These roles offer aviation careers without flight-school debt — and internal movement is real at most airlines.
learn: Learn the hiring cycles at major and regional carriers
Understand seniority-based bidding and schedules
Practice customer-recovery scenarios
Note physical requirements and training timelines

detail.description: Railroading hires conductors (trained on the job, then certified) and engineers, plus maintenance-of-way and mechanical crafts — unionized, seniority-based, with demanding on-call culture.
detail.why: Rail pays strongly without degree requirements; the trade-off is unpredictable schedules, especially early.
learn: Learn conductor-trainee program structure at Class I railroads
Understand the on-call lifestyle before applying
Note the promotion path: conductor → engineer
Compare shortline vs Class I employers

detail.description: Hours-of-service rules govern drive time, breaks, and resets (ELDs enforce them electronically); planning trips around HOS is the core professional skill of long-haul driving.
detail.why: Drivers who plan HOS well deliver on time and earn more; those who don't burn hours sitting at shippers.
learn: Learn the 11-hour/14-hour/70-hour US rule structure
Plan a multi-day trip on paper around HOS
Practice split-sleeper strategies legally
Read ELD logs like a pro (yours and mentors')

detail.description: Sitting for hours, truck-stop food, and irregular sleep are the industry's occupational hazards — the drivers who last build exercise, food, and sleep systems into their routes.
detail.why: Your medical certificate and energy depend on health; healthy drivers have longer, better-paying careers.
learn: Pack a cooler system; plan food like fuel
Keep resistance bands or a folding routine in the cab
Protect sleep with blackout and noise strategies
Keep the DOT physical easy: manage the metrics

detail.description: Ladders: driver → trainer → driver-manager/dispatcher → fleet or safety manager → operations leadership; or driver → owner-operator → small fleet owner; aviation: regional → major captain by seniority.
detail.why: Transportation careers advance through records, licenses, and trust — the ladder is unusually visible and merit-based.
learn: Map the ladder at your target employer
Identify which record elements gate each rung
Set a 5-year target (desk, owner, or specialist)
Find a mentor one rung ahead

O*NET — First-Line Supervisors of Transportation Operators

detail.description: Experienced drivers become driver-trainers (teaching CDL skills and company standards), recruiting/safety staff, and CDL-school instructors — respected roles with home time.
detail.why: Teaching pays with home time and multiplies your standards across the next driver generation.
learn: Volunteer as a ride-along trainer when eligible
Learn adult-learning basics for the cab classroom
Consider CDL-school instruction as a second career
Document your training wins for promotion files

resources.title: BLS OOH — Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers

detail.description: Automation is reshaping long-haul highway legs first; local delivery, passenger transit, inspection, dispatch, and maintenance roles remain human-centered for the foreseeable future.
detail.why: Career-proofing means favoring segments where human judgment (city driving, customer contact, oversight) stays essential.
learn: Follow autonomous-trucking deployments honestly
Favor local/last-mile and oversight skills in your plan
Keep endorsements that automation can't replace soon
Retrain toward fleet/safety roles as tech matures

resources.title: BLS OOH — Transportation and Material Moving

detail.description: Union carriers (teamster-style freight, transit, parcel) offer scale wages, pensions, and seniority systems; non-union offers faster advancement and ownership flexibility. Transit and school bus are often public.
detail.why: The union-vs-nonunion choice shapes pay curve, benefits, and work rules for a whole career — worth comparing with real numbers.
learn: Compare union vs nonunion pay at your target segment
Understand seniority systems before joining
Note pension and health-plan differences
Talk to drivers with 10+ years on each side
